## Web Searcher: academic / perceptual foundations of data encoding

Research question: "Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules."

Your angle: **academic / perceptual foundations of data encoding** — Area 1's measured core: which encodings are accurate and why, and how to build color scales that survive CVD and non-color-encoding requirements. Targets peer-reviewed HCI/vis (Cleveland & McGill 1984, Harrower & Brewer, IEEE VIS colormap work) so every claimed perceptual ranking or threshold has a citable origin rather than folklore.
Search query: `Cleveland McGill graphical perception ranking position length angle area color accuracy study, perceptually uniform OKLCH sequential and diverging colormap construction, ColorBrewer Viridis colorblind-safe palette research`

## Task
Use WebSearch with the query above (or a refined version). Return the top 4-6 most relevant results.
Rank by relevance to the ORIGINAL question, not just the search query. Skip obvious SEO spam/content farms.
Include a short snippet capturing why each result is relevant.

Structured output only.

{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"SubagentStart","additionalContext":"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

- _gstack-command: Router for the gstack skill suite. (gstack)
- academic-paper-composer: Systematic writing framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers from optimized outline to submission-ready manuscript. Use when users want to: (1) write a paper from a detailed outline, (2) ensure quality control during writing, (3) maintain consistency across chapters, (4) prepare a submission-ready manuscript, or (5) systematically execute a planned paper. Triggered by phrases like 'write the paper from this outline,' 'compose the full manuscript,' 'execute the outline,' or when users have completed strategic planning (academic-paper-strategist skill) and are ready to write. Takes optimized outline as input; outputs complete manuscript with iterative quality checks.
- academic-paper-strategist: Systematic strategic planning framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers targeting preprint platforms (PhilArchive, arXiv, PhilSci-Archive). Use when users want to: (1) plan a paper on a specific topic, (2) identify research gaps and assess originality, (3) develop optimized paper outlines, (4) prepare for preprint submission, or (5) understand platform requirements and writing standards. Triggered by phrases like 'plan a paper on,' 'help me design a paper about,' 'identify research gaps in,' 'is this idea original,' or when users need structured research planning. The skill guides through three phases: Platform Analysis (identifying target venue and studying sample papers), Theoretical Framework (AI-driven literature search and gap identification), and Outline Optimization (structured design with reviewer-perspective self-assessment). Each phase includes quality evaluation standards and validation checkpoints. Output: optimized detailed outline ready for systematic writing (use with academic-paper-composer skill).
- apify-ultimate-scraper: Universal AI-powered web scraper for any platform. Scrape data from Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, LinkedIn, X/Twitter, Google Maps, Google Search, Google Trends, Reddit, Airbnb, Yelp, and 15+ more platforms. Use for lead generation, brand monitoring, competitor analysis, influencer discovery, trend research, content analytics, audience analysis, review analysis, SEO intelligence, recruitment, or any data extraction task.

Also use when the user says "write copy for," "improve this copy," "rewrite this page," "marketing copy," "headline help," or "CTA copy." For email copy, see email-sequence. For visually important web tasks, it must first generate the design image(s) itself, deeply analyze them, then implement the website to match them as closely as possible. By default, screens should be shown inside a subtle premium iPhone or similar phone mockup with a visible frame, while the main focus stays on the app content itself. CRITICAL OUTPUT RULE — generate ONE separate horizontal image FOR EVERY section. A landing page with 8 sections produces 8 images. Never compress multiple sections into one image. ## Cleveland and McGill 1984 Experiment

In 1984, Cleveland and his colleague Robert McGill published the seminal paper Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods.

### Ranking of Elementary Perceptual Tasks

The study produced six ranked categories: 1. Position along a common scale 2. Positions along nonaligned scales 3. Length, direction, angle 4. Area 5. Volume, curvature 6. Shading, colour saturation

### Experimental Findings

Two types of position judgments were found to be the most accurate, length judgments were second, angle and slope judgments were third, and area judgments were last.

To study how humans decode graphs, Cleveland and McGill summarized ten elementary graphical encodings from various commonly-used plots and charts, and to evaluate the effectiveness of these visual encodings, they conducted two experiments using bar and pie charts.

### Significance

This paper, which has now been cited thousands of times by academics, remains a touchstone for data visualization researchers and practitioners.

## Key Findings:

**Viridis Development:**
Viridis was designed by Stéfan van der Walt and Nathaniel Smith for Matplotlib 1.5 to fix the perceptual problems of jet. The primary criterion in developing Parula and Viridis was to ensure the default colourmaps are perceptually uniform.

**Perceptual Uniformity:**
Perceptual uniformity means that if we take a small step along the path of the palette in HCL space, the perceived difference between the two colors will be the same anywhere along the path. Equal Euclidean distances between values in color space leads to an equal color difference perception, enabling the straightforward creation of perceptually uniform colormaps.

**Colorblind-Safe Design:**
Viridis is perceptually uniform, colorblind-safe, and prints well in grayscale. Fabio Crameri's Scientific Colour Maps, introduced in a 2020 Nature Communications paper, are perceptually uniform and color-blind safe by construction.

**ColorBrewer:**
ColorBrewer develops numerous attractive, perceptually uniform, and easily distinguished colourmaps. ColorBrewer is the longest-running free generator for sequential, diverging, and qualitative palettes.

## Publication Information
The paper "The misuse of colour in science communication" was published by Crameri, F., Shephard, G. E., & Heron, P. J. in Nature Communications, volume 11, article 5444, in October 2020.

## Main Focus
The paper addresses how colour maps that visually distort data through uneven colour gradients or are unreadable to those with colour-vision deficiency remain prevalent in science, including rainbow-like and red–green colour maps.

## Key Contributions
The authors present a simple guide for the scientific use of colour and show how scientifically derived colour maps report true data variations, reduce complexity, and are accessible for people with colour-vision deficiencies.

The paper highlights ways for the scientific community to identify and prevent the misuse of colour in science, and calls for a proactive step away from colour misuse among the community, publishers, and the press.

## Associated Resources
The work is connected to the Scientific Colour Maps initiative, which provides colour-blind friendly and accurate palettes available in multiple software formats including MATLAB, Python, R, GMT, QGIS, and many visualization tools.

Based on the search results, here's information about the Heer and Bostock 2010 paper:

## Overview

Jeffrey Heer and Michael Bostock published "Crowdsourcing Graphical Perception: Using Mechanical Turk to Assess Visualization Design" in ACM Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI) in 2010 and it was a Best Paper Nominee.

## Research Design

The paper assessed the viability of Amazon's Mechanical Turk as a platform for graphical perception experiments and replicated previous studies of spatial encoding and luminance contrast. Specifically, Heer and Bostock replicated ranking on effectiveness of visual encodings, such as length, position, and angle, using an alternative crowdsourced subject pool on Amazon Mechanical Turk, and further extended the study on additional encodings, such as circular area (e.g., bubble charts) and rectangular area (e.g., treemaps).

## Key Findings

The papers replicated Cleveland & McGill's original study, asking participants to compare two values using different types of visual encodings including position encoding (scatter plot), length encoding (bar chart), angle encoding (pie charts), and area encoding (bubble charts). The crowdsourced results proved that position encoding is the most accurate, length encoding is less accurate than position encoding, and angle encoding and area encoding were the least accurate.

## Significance

Crowdsourcing has become an established method for visualization research since Heer and Bostock's seminal work, which demonstrated that crowdsourced studies could replicate laboratory results from Cleveland and McGill with acceptable variation at significantly lower costs.

Based on the search results, I found the publication you're looking for:

Harrower, M., & Brewer, C. A. (2003). ColorBrewer.org: An online tool for selecting colour schemes for maps. Cartographic Journal, 40(1), 27-37.

The paper addresses the challenge that choosing effective colour schemes for thematic maps is surprisingly difficult. ColorBrewer is an online tool designed to help users select appropriate colour schemes for their specific mapping needs by considering: the number of data classes; the nature of their data (matched with sequential, diverging and qualitative schemes); and the end-use environment for the map (e.g., CRT, LCD, printed, projected, photocopied).

ColorBrewer contains 'learn more' tutorials to help guide users, prompts them to test-drive colour schemes as both map and legend, and provides output in five colour specification systems.

Links: [{"title":"Chroma-gated, differentiable OKLCH interpolation: Continuous Oklab fallback for color-cast reduction","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.15352"},{"title":"OKLCH Color Space: The Developer's Guide to Perceptually Uniform Color — ColorArchive Guides","url":"https://colorarchive.org/guides/oklch-color-space-guide/"},{"title":"OKLCH Color Picker - Modern CSS Color Space Tool","url":"https://oklch.org/"},{"title":"oklab() | CSS-Tricks","url":"https://css-tricks.com/almanac/functions/o/oklab/"},{"title":"OKLCH Color — The Modern Perceptually Uniform Color Space","url":"https://colors.jarhalab.com/wiki/oklch-color"},{"title":"Perceptual Color Spaces: Lab, LCH, Oklab, OKLCH — ColorFYI","url":"https://colorfyi.com/blog/perceptual-color-spaces/"},{"title":"Why OKLCH makes better CSS gradients · uicorn","url":"https://uicorn.com/guides/01-oklch-css-gradients/"},{"title":"Oklch+: A Three-Parameter Extension of Oklab for Improved Color Difference Prediction","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.05255"}]

Here are the search results for your query about Ottosson, Oklab, OKLCH, and CSS Color gradients:

## Key Findings

**Oklab and OKLCH Design**

Oklab is a perceptual color space designed by Ottosson for image-processing and interpolation use, fitting a lightness/opponent representation to perceptual data so that Euclidean operations behave reasonably. OKLCH is its cylindrical form, replacing the opponent pair (a, b) with chroma and hue.

**CSS Color 4 Adoption**

CSS Color 4 adopts these spaces and recommends OKLCH as an interpolation space for gradients and color-mix(). The motivation for interpolating in OKLCH rather than Oklab is hue control: a constant-chroma sweep in h follows the arc a designer expects, whereas a straight (a, b) segment cuts across it and desaturates.

**Hue Uniformity Advantages**

Oklab (2020) was designed by Björn Ottosson to fix Lab's hue non-linearity, using empirical human-perception data. It achieves better hue consistency across the chroma range. OKLCH gradients through the blue-violet range stay more vibrant and hue-stable than LCH gradients.

**Gradient Interpolation**

When CSS interpolates between two OKLCH colors, it travels through the color space along the shortest path for each of L, C, and H. Because the space is uniform, the midpoint is guaranteed to be visually halfway — not numerically halfway in sRGB.

I found information about the paper you're looking for. The article "Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods" was authored by Cleveland, W.S. and McGill, R. and published in the Journal of the American Statistical Association in 1984, volume 79, pages 531-554.

I found one direct PDF link in the search results: `http://faculty.washington.edu/aragon/classes/hcde511/s12/readings/cleveland84.pdf`

There's also a reference to the paper available through the Taylor & Francis Online platform (the official publisher of JASA): `https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478080`

The paper's approach is based on graphical perception—the visual decoding of information encoded on graphs—and includes both theory and experimentation. The theory identifies a set of elementary perceptual tasks carried out when people extract quantitative information from graphs, and orders these tasks based on how accurately people perform them.

results.title: Cleveland & McGill (1984), "Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods", JASA 79(387):531-554
results.snippet: THE primary source for the perceptual ranking the pipeline needs to cite instead of folklore. Full text PDF of the JASA paper that defines the elementary perceptual tasks and orders them by measured decoding accuracy: (1) position along a common scale, (2) position along non-aligned scales, (3) length / direction / angle, (4) area, (5) volume / curvature, (6) shading and colour saturation. Also the origin of the bar-vs-pie result (position/length beat angle) and of the dot-plot-over-pie recommendation. Any STYLES.md or CRAFT.md line claiming 'position is the most accurate encoding' should attribute here, with the caveat that the ranking is task-specific (proportion judgement of two values), not a universal law — it does not cover pattern-finding, trend, or overview tasks.

results.title: Heer & Bostock (2010), "Crowdsourcing Graphical Perception: Using Mechanical Turk to Assess Visualization Design", ACM CHI
results.snippet: The modern replication that makes the 1984 ranking citable with numbers rather than as received wisdom. Reproduces Cleveland & McGill's proportional-judgement experiment on a crowdsourced pool and extends it to encodings the original never tested — circular area (bubble charts) and rectangular area (treemaps) — confirming position < length < angle < area in log-absolute-error, and separately measuring luminance-contrast and rectangular-area (Stevens exponent) effects. Directly relevant to Area 1: gives a defensible basis for 'do not encode a quantity you want compared as bubble size', and its spatial-encoding/luminance experiments feed the non-color-encoding requirement. Web-native context too — Bostock is D3's author, so the tested stimuli are SVG-renderable.

results.title: Harrower & Brewer (2003), "ColorBrewer.org: An Online Tool for Selecting Colour Schemes for Maps", The Cartographic Journal 40(1):27-37 (refereed paper, full PDF)
results.snippet: The refereed origin of the sequential / diverging / qualitative taxonomy the pipeline is missing, and of scheme-per-class-count design. Explicitly ties scheme choice to (a) number of data classes, (b) measurement level of the data, and (c) the end-use environment — CRT, LCD, print, projection, photocopy — plus colourblind-safe and grayscale-safe flags per scheme. Directly usable: the palettes are small, fixed hex lists that can be vendored as CSS custom properties with zero byte cost and no CDN, satisfying the self-hosted constraint. Caveat to flag: ColorBrewer schemes are hand-tuned in Munsell/CIELAB-adjacent reasoning, not algorithmically perceptually uniform, and top out around 9-12 classes — for continuous ramps prefer a constructed uniform map.

results.title: Crameri, Shephard & Heron (2020), "The misuse of colour in science communication", Nature Communications 11:5444
results.snippet: Peer-reviewed evidence for the two failure modes a portfolio pipeline must avoid by rule: colour maps with uneven perceptual gradients (rainbow/jet) that manufacture false boundaries and hide real ones, and red-green pairings unreadable under colour-vision deficiency. Provides the 'Scientific colour maps' family (batlow, vik, roma, etc.), each perceptually uniform, readable in CVD simulation, and readable in grayscale — the grayscale property is the practical proof of a non-color redundant encoding. Includes a short, quotable guide plus CVD- and grayscale-simulation as a checkable acceptance test, which maps cleanly onto the pipeline's 'evidence and provenance' and 'non-color encoding' constraints.

results.title: Nuñez, Anderton & Renslow (2018), "Optimizing colormaps with consideration for color vision deficiency to enable accurate interpretation of scientific data", PLOS ONE 13(7):e0199239
results.snippet: Shows the *construction method*, not just a palette list: the authors state the optimisation objective (monotonic, near-linear lightness ramp in CAM02-UCS; minimal perceptual distortion under deuteranomaly simulation) and derive cividis from viridis by it. This is the citable answer to 'how do you build a sequential scale rather than pick one', and it documents the honest trade — viridis is colourblind-*friendly* but still uses a blue-to-yellow-green path that shifts under CVD, while cividis is optimised so a CVD and non-CVD viewer read near-identical structure. Useful for the pipeline because the same objective (monotone L*, controlled C and H) is directly expressible in OKLCH in CSS, so bespoke per-run scales can be generated instead of reusing a recognisable stock ramp — supporting the anti-template rule.

results.title: W3C, CSS Color Module Level 4 — oklab()/oklch(), color interpolation and gradient interpolation spaces
results.snippet: The normative, web-native bridge from the perceptual-colour literature to shippable CSS. Defines oklab()/oklch() (Ottosson's Oklab, fitted to perceptual data so Euclidean distance approximates perceived difference and hue stays stable across chroma), and specifies interpolation behaviour for gradients and color-mix(), including hue-interpolation methods for the cylindrical form. Practical consequences for the pipeline: perceptually uniform sequential and diverging ramps become a few CSS declarations (near-zero bytes, no runtime, no chart library, degrades via @supports to sRGB stops); a diverging scale is built as two monotone-L* arms meeting at a neutral; and holding L* monotone gives the grayscale/CVD-redundant reading Crameri's test demands. Flag as CSS-native/cheap tier, and note gamut-clipping needs checking against display-p3 vs sRGB.
